article.overview: A sample handling system is the equipment and procedures that receive, contain, transfer, document and sub-divide lunar material after it has been collected. Its job is to keep a sample intact, uncontaminated and traceable from the point of collection until it is studied, whether that happens on the Moon, inside a lander or ascent vehicle, or in a laboratory on Earth. "Sample handling system" describes a functional class rather than one standard instrument, so this article treats it as the containment and transfer chain that begins where collection ends.
article.description: Sample handling begins once a collection device has gathered regolith or core material. The handling system moves that material into a sealed container, protects the container during closure, and carries it through whatever environment comes next: a spacecraft ascent stage, a return capsule or a curation laboratory. The work covers several separate tasks. Containment keeps the sample inside its enclosure and protects people and equipment from it. Contamination control keeps terrestrial dust, moisture and organic material away from the lunar sample. Documentation records the sample's identity, location and condition. Subdivision divides the material for distribution to different analyses. These tasks can be performed by mechanisms on a robotic spacecraft, by gloveboxes and transfer chambers in a laboratory, or by a combination of both.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a sample handling system is to preserve the scientific value of a sample. Lunar material is useful only if its composition, texture and volatile content can later be measured without being altered by handling. Apollo-era experience showed that containment and cleanliness can conflict. The Lunar Receiving Laboratory had to balance biosafety containment, which required negative-pressure gloveboxes, against ultra-clean handling, which worked best in positive-pressure nitrogen gloveboxes [1]. Handling systems therefore serve two linked applications: keeping returned material safe to handle, and keeping it chemically close to its state on the Moon so that later analyses can be trusted. Samples from permanently shadowed regions are expected to contain ices and other volatile components that need sub-zero or cryogenic preservation [4].
article.operating_principle: A sample handling system controls the sample's environment at each step. Four principles recur. The first is enclosure: the sample is kept inside a sealed container or glovebox. The second is a controlled atmosphere, such as vacuum, dry nitrogen or a cleanroom, chosen to limit oxidation, moisture and contamination. The third is mechanical transfer, in which manipulators, transfer ports or robotic mechanisms move the sample without opening the enclosure. The fourth is verification, in which the seal, identity and condition of each container are checked before the next step. The Apollo laboratory design shows the trade-offs between these principles. The first facility had to decide whether samples would be handled in a vacuum or in an inert gas, and the conflict between stringent biosafety and ultra-clean handling is described as the most difficult decision in its design history [1]. The Chang'e-5 surface system shows enclosure in robotic form. A funnel protected the container during deposition, and a sweeping action removed excess material so that the lid could close [2].
article.scientific_importance: Sample handling determines whether a returned or retrieved sample can still answer the scientific questions it was collected to address. A sample that has been contaminated, oxidised or warmed beyond its design limits may give misleading measurements, and that uncertainty cannot always be removed afterwards. The 2016 NASA analysis of the Lunar Receiving Laboratory summarises the problem as a set of technical tensions between containment and cleanliness, and between particulate and organic cleanliness [1]. Lunar samples are finite and are studied for decades, so the handling system also determines how many scientists can work on the same material without degrading it. Future missions that collect samples from different environments, including cold polar regions, will raise these demands further [4].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a sample handling system. The class ranges from a sealed sampler container and sealing mechanism on a robotic spacecraft to a multi-room laboratory complex. The examples below therefore describe different kinds of system, and their values should not be compared directly. Where a value was not verified in the sources checked for this article, the article says so.

examples.name: Apollo Lunar Receiving Laboratory (Houston, 1960s)
examples.status: Earth-based laboratory for receiving and examining returned Apollo samples; not a flown payload
examples.description: The Lunar Receiving Laboratory (LRL) was built in the 1960s for the Apollo programme to receive and examine returned lunar samples. It was a laboratory on Earth, not a lunar payload. Its design history is summarised as a conflict between biosafety containment and ultra-clean sample handling. That conflict led to a separate Lunar Curatorial Facility, built between 1972 and 1979. The laboratory also had to decide the sample handling environment, choosing between vacuum and inert gas.

examples.name: Planned Artemis-era sample curation handling
examples.status: Planned; not flown; presentation not opened in full
examples.description: NASA curation planning material from 2026 describes cleanrooms, custom gloveboxes for ambient and cold samples, an ultrapure nitrogen supply, and specialised containers and sample handling tools, with a phased approach to curation laboratories for later Artemis missions. Search-result excerpts state that Artemis III samples would be processed and curated at room temperature in the Apollo Labs, and that permanently shadowed region samples would likely need sub-zero or cryogenic preservation. These are planning statements.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Chang'e-5 sampler lengths are reported as about 35 cm (shovel-type) and 30 cm (coring). The Apollo laboratory and the planned curation laboratories are facilities rather than flight hardware, and no dimensions were verified for them. No representative size can be given for the class.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The Chang'e-5 sealing and packaging system is reported at 1.5 kg, including a 360 g sample container. The sample target of up to 2 kg is a design target, not a confirmed return mass. No mass was verified for the Apollo laboratory or the planned curation laboratories.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Sample handling environments are set by the material being handled. Returned lunar samples must be contained for biosafety and kept clean. Apollo-era experience shows that containment favoured negative-pressure enclosures, while ultra-clean handling favoured positive-pressure nitrogen gloveboxes [1]. Particulate control and organic contamination control can also pull in different directions, and the 2016 analysis identifies this as a separate tension from the biosafety question [1]. On the lunar surface, the reported heat tolerance of the Chang'e-5 near-field cameras is 130 °C [2]. The full thermal envelope of the sealed container was not verified. Samples from permanently shadowed regions may require sub-zero or cryogenic preservation and active cooling during transit to Earth [4].
article.limitations: A sample handling system is not one design, so the examples cannot be combined into a single performance envelope. The Apollo laboratory is a ground facility rather than lunar hardware. The Chang'e-5 figures come from a secondary popular-science account and mission news, not from a primary technical paper. The sealing mechanism, lid closure and container material for Chang'e-5 are not described in the sources checked. The planned Artemis-era systems are supported only by planning statements. Handling requirements also depend on the type of sample: dry regolith, volatile-rich polar material and biologically sensitive returned material each need different controls.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A sample handling system belongs to the sample-return category, so this section discusses containment, handling, sealing, transfer and return-chain constraints.
transportation_process: Surface integration: in the Chang'e-5 architecture, samplers collected material and cameras guided its deposit into a container, which was gripped and placed into the ascender [2]. This is a flown architecture, not a general interface other landers could reuse.

Transfer and ascent: mission reporting states that the samples were sealed in a storage device carried by the ascender, which would lift off to transfer them to the returner [3]. The ascent is reported as expected, not as a confirmed event.

Deployment and setup: a future surface system would need its sealed container and handling hardware mounted, powered and thermally protected for the surface stay. No interface requirements were verified for a named lander.

Return chain: cold or volatile-rich samples would need active cooling during transit from the Moon to a curation facility on Earth [4]. On arrival they would move into gloveboxes or cleanrooms with controlled gas, as described for planned NASA curation laboratories [4].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: For the Chang'e-5 system, a robotic sampler and manipulator deposited material into a container, which was then transferred into the ascender [2]. Methods for a future system are not verified.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo Lunar Receiving Laboratory received returned samples on Earth [1]. The Chang'e-5 surface sampling and sealing system sealed a container on the surface in 2020 [2][3].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with any named lander, ascender or returner is not established by the sources checked. A compatibility assessment would need the container mass and dimensions, the interface and sealing mechanism, the thermal requirements and the transfer hardware.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo missions returned samples that required a dedicated receiving and curation infrastructure, and the Lunar Receiving Laboratory was built in the 1960s for that purpose [1]. A NASA-hosted analysis by Allton reports roughly 2,200 Apollo samples totalling about 382 kg from the six landings [5]. This figure was identified from a search excerpt and was not checked in full. A separate Lunar Curatorial Facility was built between 1972 and 1979 [1]. The design tensions recorded in that history remain directly relevant to containment questions for future sample return [1][4]. The 2020 Chang'e-5 mission extended robotic surface sampling with a sealed container and an ascent transfer [2][3].
